name: Currency Hedging
title: Currency Hedging
answer: Currency hedging is the practice of reducing the effect of exchange rate movements on a company's cash flows, balance sheet values, or forecast transactions. It sits within treasury and liquidity because unhedged currency exposure can create sudden cash shortfalls or accounting volatility. The scope covers translation exposure from foreign subsidiaries, transaction exposure from payables and receivables in foreign currencies, and economic exposure from longer term competitive shifts. A treasury team typically sets a hedging policy that defines which exposures are covered, what instruments are allowed, and how much residual risk is acceptable.

sections.body: Currency hedging is the practice of reducing the effect of exchange rate movements on a company's cash flows, balance sheet values, or forecast transactions. It sits within treasury and liquidity because unhedged currency exposure can create sudden cash shortfalls or accounting volatility. The scope covers translation exposure from foreign subsidiaries, transaction exposure from payables and receivables in foreign currencies, and economic exposure from longer term competitive shifts. A treasury team typically sets a hedging policy that defines which exposures are covered, what instruments are allowed, and how much residual risk is acceptable.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Hedging runs on the treasury workstation or enterprise resource planning system where exposures are collected from subsidiaries and business units. Market data feeds for spot and forward rates, interest rate differentials, and volatility are connected to the hedging module. Execution often happens through an online trading portal with the company's banks, and confirmations, settlements, and accounting entries flow back into the general ledger. Some teams add a data warehouse or business intelligence layer to reconcile exposure forecasts against actual cash flows.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with identifying and netting exposures by currency, amount, and timing. The treasury team then chooses instruments, most commonly forward contracts, options, or cross currency swaps, to offset the identified risk. Hedge accounting under standards such as IFRS 9 or ASC 815 requires documenting the relationship between the hedged item and the hedging instrument and testing effectiveness. Regular reporting shows the mark to market value of hedges, the amount of exposure left open, and any cash margin or collateral posted.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: A hedging policy approved by the board or audit committee sets limits on instruments, counterparties, tenor, and the proportion of forecast exposure that may be hedged. Segregation of duties separates the people who propose trades, approve them, confirm them, and settle them. Counterparty credit risk is managed through bank limits and, where required, collateral agreements. Audit trails and regulatory disclosures, such as those under EMIR or Dodd Frank for derivatives, create a record of why each hedge was put on and how it was valued.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Treasury teams are moving from spreadsheet based exposure collection to automated feeds from enterprise systems, which shortens the time between exposure identification and hedge execution. Machine learning is beginning to be used for cash flow forecasting and for detecting anomalies in exposure data, though the hedging decision itself remains a controlled treasury process. Real time visibility of net open positions across currencies is becoming more common, and some firms are exploring application programming interfaces to connect treasury systems directly to bank execution platforms. The direction is toward faster, more granular hedging with stronger auditability, not toward speculative positioning.
